When posting an outage query, please note where possible:

  • POI (including CVC Link, check My Aussie or iOS and Android app)
  • Technology (FTTP, FTTN, FTTC, FTTB, HFC, Fixed Wireless, Opticomm)
  • Any local issues which may be relevant (power, recent storms/weather etc.)
  • Brief description of outage i.e. Not just internet is down
  • Any troubleshooting you may have already done, such as rebooting NBN NCD/NTD, Router etc.

tobyz writes...

Bad upload on HFC is usually attributed to faulty coax connection

And it can also be attributed to congestion within NBN on the upload...

There is only something less than 100Mbps of upload capacity (192Mbps after coexistence) per segment and initially they are adding up to 900 users per segment (will be halved eventually)....

That's one reason Telstra limited uploads on their HFC offering. Everyone suffers from contention on all services... but nothing like the amount on HFC upload.... one of the reasons for the NBN pause in installation. As they added users the HFC was going into melt down! (and with school holidays.... up goes usage.... good luck!!)

Bazzaman writes...

I turned off my router and Arris modem, waited 20 or so seconds and turned Arris modem back on. Waited till it got its connect back then restarted router. Speeds were back and webpages load fast again.

I think the equipment needs a power cycle every so offen just to refresh itself.

Hopefully someone with some serious DOCSIS 3.0 & Arris knowledge can answer, but will these cable modems change channels after startup or will it move to other channels in the case of noise, contention, etc.?

I've heard of multiple cases where bad speeds (including just upload) were due to corrosion at the tap and have heard of instances where the NBN installers put their test device on and find only some channels are impacted by noise. It is also entirely possible there is contention on the uplink, but I don't recall ever hearing of anyone hitting that other than sporadically.

Anyway, the point of my original question is that restarting the cable modem may have caused it to sync to channels that aren't as impacted by noise or interference. There is also a chance there was a transient issue in the router. It's not unheard of, but it's only been the FTTN people that seem to hit that kind of thing.

If you get the problem again, try restarting only one device and check things. Personally, I would do the router first because it's your responsibility and is a lot easier to replace than the pain of getting ISP's to convince NBN to show up or look into their network.

Noidentity writes...

But I'm not seeing any others affected. Why is that, especially as to turns out a backhaul problem... That only affects one ISP?

Telstra will have their own protection, Optus will likely use Optus cables, TPG/Internode/iinet will use pipe networks cables, and smaller providers will likely use a mixture of the above providers, and may have their own protection if using Telstra for backhaul.

So if Telstra have a link and we are on Telstra infrastructure, why isn't out traffic rerouted as well

Because Aussie BB haven't got another circuit they have purchased (yet) from Telstra to reroute to. Telstra don't manage Aussie BB's traffic, they provide circuits for Aussie BB to manage traffic on the circuit(s). Until another circuit is brought in, all that can be done is for Aussie BB to wait for Telstra to perform their repairs.

Its coming! Its one of their next projects now the big rollout to each POI was completed.

The AC68U has both a WAN DHCP client ( here one can override the obtained DNS resolvers ) and a LAN DHCP server ( where it can provide DNS resolvers to all LAN clients ).

You might wish to manually override the WAN DHCP client on the RTAC68U to:

DNS1: Google 8.8.8.8
DNS2: OpenDNS 208.67.222.222

and likewise to the LAN DHCP server on the RTAC68U, and see how it goes.

To check whether this is the issue, it's probably easiest just to change it on your desktop system. i.e. manually set the DNS servers to 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4 rather than allow it to get addresses from DHCP.

(You could change them on your router, but you're going to been to force your desktop/client system to read the new values, so it's probably just easier forcing it on your desktop system)

I guess the supplementary question is: do you see the problem on multiple systems?

I'm not sure what you mean. Techie saw I had no foxtel connection so drilled a hole and put the connection in. Bought a modem from Aussie.

He's asking whether you have a Telstra Bigpond Cable (HFC) connection going at the same time. i.e. did you have Bigpond cable before getting NBN? (I'm guessing not from what you'd said)

The only things I could recommend would be to power cycle the NBN (Arris) cable modem and make sure the coax cables are screwed in tight and the ethernet cables are clipped in properly.

When a dropout happens, take a look at the lights on the front of the NBN (Arris) cable modem. If you don't have all 4 lights on it's likely to be an NBN issue back in their network.

Anyway, if reseating / checking the cables are connected properly doesn't fix it, call ABB support so they can triage it and figure out whether to get NBN involved.

nslookup google.com <dns address>

I had the same thing previously with my HFC connection. I'm in a low signal area and during the afternoon (when the weather was hot) the upload would crawl to zero or the connection would drop out.

NBN came and replaced the tap in the street and in my box on the side of the house. The techs thought was that during the afternoon the pit would get full sun, and the combination of the sun and the ambient heat would cause the connection to drop as it was affecting the tap connection.

After the tap was replaced it's been fine so far – even during very hot weather.

Hey John et al., how do scheduled outage notifications work?

My HFC area had an unnotified 5 hour daytime outage on Wednesday. As part of my standard troubleshooting procedure, I went for a walk around the block looking for telco workers in the streets servicing my segment. I found a couple of crews. One lot were replacing a tap and said things would be back on soon (which never happened) the second crew were doing a pit replacement and said Telstra had turned off the cable for the area and it should be back by 3pm. (It ended up being not long after) The crew said it was scheduled and Telstra should have sent out notifications.

At the time there was only one outage in progress listed on ABB's site for somewhere else in Australia. When I went to Telstra's site (which makes you put in your address) it said there was a cable outage in progress for my location and gave an ETA. I decided to check a TPG outage site and it listed a couple of outages for my suburb (with no specific location info) but said it was scheduled and gave a time frame of 7am-3pm (which is a pretty standard for Telstra work). There were also quite a few listed for other parts of Australia for NBN that looked similar.

I didn't get any notification of an outage, which makes me think something is broken somewhere, or could be improved.

Interestingly, ABB sent me warning email on 12-Dec passing on a NBN warning of an overnight 4 hour outage that would impact me on 11-Jan somewhere in a 7 hour window. From what I can tell I didn't see an interruption in service, unless it was only minutes long.

Looking at ABB's site, my POI is listed for a scheduled outage on 8-Feb (which I assume is an ABB rather than upstream outage). I haven't received an email about that (yet).

So, back to the original point of the question, is this normal (i.e. you don't have an automated system in place yet, hence pester Phil for a "next big thing") or is there a broken notification system somewhere (e.g. ABB, NBN, Telstra, etc)?

I guess my expectation is that I'd like a notification (in advance) for scheduled outages.

Whim me if you want location details as I have a few services in my name.

Thanks!

We automatically send out email outage notices from NBN when we receive them. If it is a cable outage that NBN didn't tell us about then we won't know and it won't be sent. The outages on our website are for backhaul or AussieBB planned (and unplanned) outages.

oodLes writes...

You need to get a backup connection dude. 4G Plan with the option to add a data pack or similar if its crucial to your business.

That is what we had to do as we have our own clients to support. We have to provide the redundancy because NBN / Telstra / Aussie or whoever fault all these long outages are does not. It was not cheap to setup with a CISCO router but we now have auto failover to very expensive 4G bandwidth. Even then it means our static WAN IP changes which limits what we can do, our bandwidth is also much lower especially upstream.

In the past we had ADSL and for several years dual ISDN ... we use to be able to login to our servers (SSH sessions) and the sessions would last weeks or months. Never did we have any hour-long outages. I think we had 1 outage with Dual ISDN in 5 years and just for 30 minutes. Uptime with the NBN and Aussie has been absolutely terrible. Many hours long outages both planned and unplanned. Things have gone backwards in respect to uptime with the NBN. When it is working it great but there are clearly problems with uptime.
